findings.text: The `if not hasattr(cls, "__rich_repr__")` guard is also true for inherited methods, so a subclass decorated with `@auto(angular=True)` whose parent was already decorated never gets the `angular` flag set. It keeps the parent's flag and renders as `Child(...)` instead of `<Child ...>`. The same happens when the class defines its own `__rich_repr__` without an `angular` attribute, because the decorator argument is silently ignored.

`auto_rich_repr` turns any failure into `ReprError`, and `repr()` now propagates it. For `@auto class A: def __init__(self, x): self._x = x`, `getattr(self, 'x')` fails and `repr(a)` raises `ReprError` instead of returning a string. This breaks logging, debuggers and tracebacks. The old `rich_repr` only ever used a user-written `__rich_repr__`.

`param.default == param.empty` uses `==` instead of `is`. A default whose `__eq__` returns a non-bool, such as a numpy array, makes the `if` raise and the repr fails. `auto_repr` also does `default[0] == value`, which breaks the same way. `*args` and `**kwargs` parameters are silently dropped from the generated repr.

0.reason: At repr.py:119, `hasattr` also finds an inherited `__rich_repr__` or one the class defines itself, so the angular flag is only set when the auto method is installed; in those other cases `@auto(angular=True)` is silently ignored and the repr comes out as `Child(...)`.

1.reason: The `ReprError` is raised on purpose (a dedicated exception class with explicit wrapping), so an `__init__` parameter with no matching attribute fails loudly by design; this is not an accidental defect.
